list-item.p: There is increasing evidence that patient-reported outcomes following total knee arthroplasty (TKA) are associated with psychosocial factors and pain catastrophizing. Sleep disturbance, pain, and mental health have a complex interaction, which, if unrecognized, can be associated with impaired patient-reported outcomes and dissatisfaction following TKA.
The gold standard of objective sleep assessment is polysomnography, which is not feasible to use routinely for TKA patients. Wearable devices are a validated and less costly alternative.

Subjective sleep measures, such as the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, or Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) computerized adaptive test sleep domains, are simple to administer and provide additional insight into sleep disturbance. Although objective and subjective measures do not correlate precisely, they can be informative together.

Sleep disturbances in the elderly population are common and multifactorial in etiology, stemming from the interplay of sleep disorders, medication side effects, and pain. Commonly prescribed medications following TKA as well as postoperative pain can exacerbate underlying sleep disturbances.

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is prevalent in patients seeking TKA. In the setting of OSA, postoperative opioids can cause respiratory depression, resulting in consequences as severe as death. A standardized multimodal pain protocol including anti-inflammatories and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) analogues may allow for decreased reliance on opioids for pain control.

Surgeons should reassure patients that postoperative sleep disturbance is common and transient, collaborate with the patient’s primary care doctor to address sleep disturbance, and avoid prescription of pharmaceutical sleep aids.

body.p: Enhanced perioperative care through multimodal pain management and physical therapy protocols has enabled surgeons to safely decrease hospital length of stay and improve the rate of early functional recovery following total knee arthroplasty (TKA)1. Despite these improvements, recovery after TKA remains prolonged for most patients, with subjective measures of patient well-being lagging behind objective measures of physical function2-5. Beyond 1 year, 10% to 20% of patients may remain dissatisfied with TKA despite the absence of any discernable technical shortcoming6-9.

There is increasing recognition of the impact that psychological patient-related factors can have on recovery and outcomes after TKA, which may account for this discrepancy between surgeon satisfaction with the procedural performance and patient satisfaction10-12. Sleep is an important physiologic process involved in both physical and mental health. Sleep disturbances or diagnosis of a formal sleep disorder, defined as a condition that affects sleep quality, timing, or duration, is common both in patients with end-stage knee osteoarthritis (OA) and patients recovering after TKA13-17. Poor sleep has far-reaching associations with mental health disorders, including anxiety and depression, pain sensitization, paranoia, hallucinations, and relationship distress18-22. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common and potentially lethal sleep disorder, and we must be aware of the condition. OSA, when combined with typical postoperative narcotics following TKA, may result in respiratory depression and endanger our patients following TKA, even if the disorder was controlled preoperatively23,24.

Given the high rate of sleep disturbances and disorders among patients with knee osteoarthritis and those undergoing TKA, it is important for the practicing arthroplasty surgeon to have an understanding of these topics13-15. The purpose of this review was to provide a primer on sleep physiology and normal sleep architecture, define the most common sleep disorders that affect TKA patients, and review the current literature on the management of sleep apnea and sleep disturbance after TKA. Increased awareness of these topics should improve perioperative management, patient optimization prior to TKA, and patient satisfaction and recovery postoperatively.

sec.title: Sleep Physiology
sec.p: Sleep is a rapidly reversible behavioral state, characterized by unresponsiveness to the environment, that is mediated by a complex array of multiple anatomical structures in the brain and interacting neurotransmitters that are controlled by a 2-process model25.

First, a homeostatic process (Process S) leads to an increased sleep drive during prolonged wakefulness25. During a typical 8-hour sleep, the brain’s electrical activity cycles through states of nonrapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep26. Sleep stage timing and duration vary during the night, with 3 stages of NREM sleep, which represent a continuum of relative depth, occurring predominantly in the first half of the night and REM sleep occurring in the latter half26,27. As humans age, stage-1 and 2 sleep increases while REM sleep decreases28,29.

Second, a circadian process (Process C) opposes the homeostatic process, preventing sleep during the day but allowing for consolidated sleep at night25. Circadian rhythms are “entrained” by numerous factors, with light being the strongest timekeeper30. Others include social interactions, timing of meals, physical activity, and plasma melatonin levels26. “Clock” genes control the sleep-wake cycle, modulate physical activity and food consumption, as well as regulate body temperature, heart rate, muscle tone, and hormone secretion31. This cycle is critical to promote the formation of memories, removal of toxins, muscle repair, growth, and immune function, and it plays a role in bone health32.

sec.title: Objective Sleep Measures
sec.p: Objective sleep data such as polysomnography and in-home sleep studies are useful for understanding sleep disturbances, but they can be challenging to obtain (Table I)33,34. Consumer “wearables” have emerged as a reliable and accessible objective method of sleep monitoring33-36. Several advanced multisensory consumer devices, or wearables, have been developed and are now being worn by hundreds of millions of people around the world33. These are low-cost accelerometers that measure movement and have been proposed as a more accessible alternative to actigraphy or polysomnography37-42. Polysomnography is the gold standard for monitoring sleep-wake activity, and it allows for assessment of sleep staging, sleep-related breathing events, and other sleep phenomena via electroencephalography, electromyography, oximetry, airflow sensors, respiratory effort belts, and other sensors. In comparison with traditional monitoring systems, several consumer devices (Fatigue Science ReadiBand, Fitbit Alta HR, EarlySense Live, ResMed S+, and SleepScore Max [SleepScore Labs]) performed as well as or better than actigraphy in detecting sleep and wakefulness, and as with actigraphy, they demonstrated a high sensitivity in detecting sleep but less accuracy in detecting wakefulness than polysomnography33,43,44. We do not recommend any formal routine postoperative objective sleep monitoring, although many patients may already be utilizing a consumer wearable device that may be used to provide useful sleep information.

sec.title: Subjective Sleep Measures
sec.p: A variety of patient questionnaires have been used to assess patients’ subjective sleep experience in the setting of knee osteoarthritis or TKA. The Epworth Sleepiness Scale is an 8-question survey aimed at determining the level of daytime sleepiness45. The insomnia severity index is a 7-question survey taking into account the patient’s dissatisfaction and worry about their current sleep pattern46. The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) is a more involved, 19-item survey with component scores of subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, use of sleeping medication, and daytime dysfunction47,48. The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) has 2 domains relevant to sleep: Sleep-Related Impairment, which measures alertness, sleepiness, tiredness, and functional impairment associated with sleep problems during waking hours, and the Sleep Disturbance questionnaire, which measures sleep quality, depth, and restoration49. Although objective and subjective measures do not correlate precisely, they can be informative together.

sec.title: Knee OA and Sleep Disturbance
sec.p: The association between knee OA and poor sleep is well established and has been shown in both clinical studies as well as experimental animal models14,50-52. Up to 31% of patients with knee OA reported difficulty with sleep onset; 18%, poor sleep quality; and 81%, trouble with sleep maintenance at least weekly53,54. The severity of radiographic OA has been correlated directly with the severity of the sleep disturbance50. While the reason for poor sleep in these patients may be multifactorial, nocturnal pain is the strongest contributing factor to sleep disturbance and generalized fatigue54-57. Additionally, pain catastrophizing, which involves a negative cognitive focus on one’s pain, has been associated with amplified pain and poor sleep15,46,58. Managing pain in patients with knee OA using acupuncture, meditation, yoga, and cognitive behavioral therapy have demonstrated subjective and objective improvements in sleep59-62.

sec.title: Epidemiology and Duration
sec.p: Patients commonly report poor sleep in the 6-week period after a TKA, noting an inability to fall asleep, nighttime arousals, and sleep disruptions45,63. By 3 to 6 months, most patients have recovered sleep back to the preoperative levels with improvements beyond the preoperative baseline at the 1-year mark45,64,65.

sec.title: Factors Affecting Postoperative Sleep
sec.p: Poor sleep after TKA is multifactorial and can be attributed to baseline sleep disturbance from surgery, primary sleep disorders, and patient-related factors, including age and comorbidities, anesthesia, metabolic response to surgery, perioperative medications, and pain50,63,66,67.

sec.title: Primary Sleep Disorders
sec.p: Common sleep disorders in the older adult population include insomnia, OSA, and restless leg syndrome (RLS) (Table II)68-70. These can be present in isolation but more commonly occur as a complex scenario involving either multiple primary sleep disorders or secondary factors. The most common form of sleep disturbance, insomnia, is diagnosed when a person experiences dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality, difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, waking too early, or having nonrestorative sleep for at least 3 nights a week for >3 months71. In 1 study, the prevalence of insomnia symptoms in adults >65 years old was 50%16.

sec.p: RLS is characterized by unpleasant sensations in the limbs causing the urge to move and occurs in 9% to 20% of older adults72. Immobility, anemia, and sleep disruption are known to exacerbate RLS, and all may worsen in the postoperative TKA setting73-76.

sec.title: Patient-Related Factors
sec.p: Changes in sleep physiology and psychosocial factors associated with aging as well as an increased rate of sleep disorders may precipitate sleep disturbances in the older adult population. Both sleep architecture and circadian rhythms change with age, resulting in decreased sleep efficiency, decreased slow-wave sleep, and earlier sleep onset26,77.

sec.title: Effects of Anesthesia
sec.p: There are limited data on surgical and anesthesia-related factors contributing to sleep disturbances in TKA. General anesthesia is associated with postoperative worsening of the apnea-hypopnea index in patients with OSA as well as substantially worse sleep on the night of surgery78,79. With spinal and neuraxial anesthesia, as opposed to general anesthesia, airway instrumentation can be avoided and medications acting centrally can be used sparingly, which may be beneficial in the setting of OSA80.

sec.title: Perioperative Medications
sec.p: Medications commonly used in the older population, such as beta-blockers, pseudoephedrine, corticosteroids, and certain antidepressants, have demonstrated deleterious effects on sleep81. Not only can medications result in direct sleep disturbance, but they can also indirectly cause sleep-disrupting symptoms, such as coughing, dyspnea, dyspepsia, urinary frequency, or nocturnal hypoglycemia81,82.

Methylprednisolone can be used after TKA to attenuate the inflammatory response. In a randomized clinical trial of 48 patients, use of a single dose of preoperative methylprednisolone worsened sleep quality but lessened fatigue83. Chronic opioid use decreases REM sleep, increases waking in the middle of the night, and worsens respiratory depression84-86. When nonopioid medications, such as cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitors and pregabalin, are added to the postoperative pain management course, less narcotic pain medication is used and, thus, there is less sleep disturbance87-89. Surgeons should continue to look toward other modes of pain management to decrease narcotic use and thereby improve initial sleep disturbance.

sec.title: Pain
sec.p: Pain and sleep disturbance have a complex relationship following TKA. In a small cohort of 24 patients who underwent TKA, greater pain intensity and level of disability after TKA were correlated with worse sleep quality90. Interestingly, despite pain consistently decreasing over all time points following TKA, the PSQI scores worsened until 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively and required 3 months to improve past baseline13,65.

sec.title: Association with Outcomes
sec.p: There has been minimal research performed on the negative association that sleep has with outcomes after TKA. Sleep disruptions at 1 month predict 3-month functional limitations63. In a study of 780 patients undergoing arthroplasty (48% had TKA), the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), as well as health-related quality of life (EuroQol-5 Dimensions [EQ-5D]), was weakly correlated with sleep quality and duration both before and after surgery91. In addition, those who endorsed “good sleep” endorsed higher satisfaction with the surgery91.

sec.title: Interventions for Improving Sleep After TKA
Nonpharmacologic Sleep Interventions
sec.p: Cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBTi) uses multiple nonpharmacologic interventions to treat insomnia and has been shown to improve short and long-term sleep92. Interventions include creating a mild sleep deprivation state followed by slowly increasing the time in bed until optimal duration is achieved, relaxation training, cognitive restructuring, and sleep hygiene education68,92. Unfortunately, traditional methods of CBTi can be challenging to access for patients, given the overwhelming number of patients with sleep issues, limited CBTi providers, as well as the typical 8-week course of therapy required to see effects68,92. Patients may become discouraged without seeing immediate improvement, as often occurs with those who expect a quick effect from therapy. Similar to discussions of therapy, we should encourage patience in achieving results as there is no overnight solution for these long-standing issues. Mindfulness-based stress reduction techniques have also been effective in an older adult population93. These techniques use breathing and meditations targeting awareness and acceptance of the present state94. There are more accessible commercial as well as free apps that assist patients with a mindfulness or sleep regimen, which are detailed in Table III. A study of self-guided meditation through the use of a video following TKA demonstrated that patients who used the video gained nearly an hour of additional sleep and had fewer awakenings95. Bright light therapy, acupuncture, and music listening at bedtime have also demonstrated positive results in older patients96-98.

sec.title: Pharmacologic Sleep Aids
sec.p: Several drug classes are commonly used to treat sleep disturbances. We introduce these as a means of understanding the mechanisms and risks of these medications that patients are commonly taking or requesting perioperatively. In general, they provide little to no benefit in improving sleep after TKA and have substantial side-effect profiles that can lead to complications99. We recommend against orthopaedic surgeons routinely prescribing these medications.

sec.title: Benzodiazepines
sec.p: Benzodiazepines should be prescribed with caution as they can result in dependence, addiction, memory impairment, falls, fractures, and hospital admissions100-102. After TKA, benzodiazepines are a known risk factor for complications, including postoperative delirium (odds ratio [OR], 2.47; 95% confidence interval, 2.04 to 2.97)103.

sec.title: Nonbenzodiazepine Hypnotics
sec.p: Nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics such as zolpidem (Ambien), in a study of 20 patients following TKA and total hip arthroplasty (THA), did not demonstrate any significant difference in sleep parameters from placebo but did demonstrate subjective improvements in fatigue and sleep quality and a decrease in the number of arousals104. However, these medications have been shown to cause confusion, resulting in an increased risk of falls and fractures105.

sec.title: Melatonin
sec.p: Melatonin and melatonin receptor agonists (ramelteon) have not shown the same negative effects as the previously listed medications; however, the use of melatonin has not demonstrated improvement in the PSQI following TKA or THA compared with placebo47.

sec.title: Antidepressants and Antihistamines
sec.p: Antidepressants (trazodone) and antihistamines (hydroxyzine and diphenhydramine) are commonly prescribed in the postoperative period. Both groups of medications have been associated with falls in older adults and have not been studied in patients following TKA106.

We do not recommend routinely initiating a pharmacologic sleep aid postoperatively, given the lack of supportive data for any medication listed above. Interventions studied to improve sleep following TKA are described in the Appendix, and our recommendations for managing sleep following TKA are given in Table IV.

sec.title: Epidemiology
sec.p: Sometimes sleep disturbances are a result of a formal sleep disorder. OSA is repetitive airway collapse during sleep that causes hypoxemia, arousal from sleep, and daytime sleepiness. The prevalence of OSA in patients undergoing TKA has been reported to be as much as 70%107-110. Older patients, males, and obese patients are at higher risk, with up to 51% of patients presenting for TKA with undiagnosed OSA106,111-114. It is paramount for arthroplasty surgeons to recognize risk factors and to screen and manage patients appropriately for this condition.

sec.title: Preoperative Screening
sec.p: All patients undergoing elective TKA, especially those undergoing same-day surgery, should be screened for OSA with the simple STOP-BANG (Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnea, high blood Pressure-Body mass index [BMI], Age, Neck circumference, and Gender) questionnaire78,115,116. This simple questionnaire involves 8 binary questions regarding snoring, tiredness during daytime, observed apnea, high blood pressure, BMI, age, neck circumference, and male gender. With a STOP-BANG score of 5, a patient has a 50% probability of moderate to severe OSA and a 30% probability of severe OSA117. If scoring is consistent with OSA, the surgery may still proceed with the assumption that the patient has OSA, and appropriate measures are taken115. Those with preexisting OSA with a continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) machine should bring the mask with them to surgery and wear it postoperatively. If the STOP-BANG score is ≥2, serious consideration should be given to referring the patient for a preoperative sleep study and subsequently to a pulmonologist if the apnea-hypopnea index is >20118.

sec.title: Perioperative Management and Considerations
sec.p: Perioperative management of patients with OSA requires special considerations. Neuraxial and regional anesthesia are preferred in patients with OSA to decrease opioid use and avoid the neuromuscular blockade and airway manipulation associated with general anesthesia119. Postoperative management of these patients must take into account their predisposition for drug-induced respiratory depression, which can be life-threatening, especially in the setting of postoperative opioid or benzodiazepine use106. Opioids should be limited in patients with OSA, but this is complicated by the hyperalgesia and increased analgesic requirements often seen in this group as a result of sleep fragmentation and intermittent hypoxia120. Early incentive spirometer use, avoidance of narcotics, spinal anesthesia, aspiration precautions, keeping the head of the bed elevated, as well as maintaining oxygen saturation above 92% are useful in minimizing pulmonary complications following TKA118,121. Prior to discharge, patients should be able to maintain adequate oxygen saturation while asleep breathing room air, or those who use a CPAP machine preoperatively should maintain oxygen saturation while using this device postoperatively prior to discharge115.

sec.title: Impact on Outcomes
sec.p: Sleep apnea has a negative effect on the perioperative safety and short and long-term outcomes of TKA. Sleep apnea is associated with postoperative delirium in TKA patients as well as a higher risk of inpatient falls66,122. In a cohort of >1,000 patients, OSA was associated with dissatisfaction following TKA (OR = 1.82; p = 0.04)123. Sleep apnea has been shown to correlate with increased cost and complications after TKA, with a medical complication OR of 3.71 compared with patients without OSA124. Implant failure, readmission rates, and overall costs for TKA patients are associated with OSA125.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Functional limitations, greater pain intensity, and poor sleep quality are correlated following TKA. Our older adult patients have many reasons to have a sleep disturbance perioperatively, often including at least 1 sleep disorder. The literature currently lacks solutions for these patients. We recommend counseling patients preoperatively about expected postoperative sleep disturbances, and key points for patient education should be discussed (Table III). We recommend screening all patients preoperatively for insomnia, RLS, and OSA and following the flowchart in Figure 1 if these diagnoses are identified. Although CBTi may be the optimal treatment for insomnia, this standard may be unachievable for many patients. Alternatively, educating patients about techniques such as mindfulness, as well as setting expectations for postoperative sleep disturbances may provide them with a more attainable solution. The greatest predictor of dissatisfaction following TKA in at least 1 study was unmet expectations2. With this in mind, it is important to discuss with patients the fact that a sleep disturbance is exceedingly common after TKA and that it typically resolves within 3 months postoperatively.

sec.title: Future Directions
sec.p: The first step in improving sleep following TKA is recognizing that, as orthopaedic surgeons, a successful patient outcome requires more than perfect radiographs and a stable knee with excellent range of motion and appropriate alignment. It has become clear over the past decade that patient-reported outcomes are affected by a variety of psychosocial factors as well as sleep. It is possible that sleep quality may prove to be a surrogate for a satisfactory result following TKA63. Despite patient-reported outcomes being a focus following TKA, and many of our patients having reported sleep disturbances following TKA, there is a paucity of effective treatments for improving sleep after TKA. A future focus should be on identifying medications or nonpharmacologic interventions to improve sleep and thus overall patient satisfaction following TKA.
